text.p: The battered Japanese stock market took another tumble Monday, depressed by the government's unwavering resolve to raise taxes and by the bankruptcy of a once high-flying chain of sushi bars.

The key Nikkei average of 225 leading shares sank more than 800 points in early trading as investors gambled that a policy speech by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto later in the day would fail to deliver any boost for stocks.

As expected, the government resisted calls from the stock market to reconsider its economic policies, offering no special relief for the market and vowing to press ahead with tax increases. But the index clawed back a little, ending down 609.70 points at 17,480.34.
The latest fall in Japanese stocks helped push the U.S. dollar to a 46-month high of 117.90 yen, partly on fears that the weakness would cause foreign investors to sell the Japanese currency.

In his policy speech to the new session of parliament, Hashimoto vowed to forge ahead with a rise in the sales tax to 5 percent from 3 percent on April 1 and end two trillion Japanese yen ($17 billion) worth of special income tax cuts. He also warned that more belt-tightening was in store, but announced no new measures or revisions to previously announced plans.

Stocks started the day on a sombre note after a chain of sushi restaurants said it was seeking protection from creditors under Japan's bankruptcy laws, joining a growing list of companies crushed by big debts.
The move underlined the extent of the economic woes left over from the late 1980s bubble of aggressive expansion, soaring asset prices and unbridled consumerism.

Kyotaru Co. Ltd. filed for protection Sunday with huge debts totalling $865 million, becoming the first failure among firms listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange since mid-1993. The chain had expanded abroad and invested heavily in the 1980s and struggled to restructure when the bubble burst in the early 1990s.
Traders said the stock slide was mostly led by a futures sell-off, which signalled the market's disapproval of Hashimoto's anticipated policy statement.

The stock market has fallen heavily since the start of the year on worries about the health of the banking industry and fears that the proposed tax increases could strangle Japan's tentative economic recovery.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita Monday attempted to calm those fears, telling a central bank branch managers' meeting that Japan's economy was still gradually recovering and that the strength of the recovery was growing gradually.
On the foreign exchange market, the slide in stock prices prompted selling of Japanese yen by overseas operators.
But dealers said the greatest action in the dollar was against the German mark, where massive bids by overseas traders, particularly U.S. funds, sent the dollar surging.
